meta.title: AI Email Connectors vs MCP Server: How the Two Approaches Differ
meta.description: Two ways to give an AI assistant your inbox: a connector built into one assistant, or an MCP email server you connect yourself. How they differ on mailbox reach, multiple inboxes, portability, and who holds the credentials.

hero.titleLine1: Two ways to give an AI
hero.lead: A connector built into an assistant is the shortest path when it covers your mail provider. An MCP email server is a separate service you connect yourself: it reaches any mailbox that speaks IMAP and SMTP, holds several inboxes at once, and works in every MCP client. Here is how the two approaches differ, structurally.

axes.title: Where the two approaches diverge
axes.sub: Not a feature scoreboard. These differences follow from how each approach is built, so they hold whatever capabilities any vendor ships.

coverage.p: A built-in connector reaches the mail providers its vendor has integrated. IMAP and SMTP are open protocols your mailbox already speaks, whoever runs it, so one connection covers Fastmail, iCloud, Yahoo, Zoho, Yandex, Migadu, a server your company runs, or one you host yourself. Gmail connects over OAuth.

inboxes.h: A workspace, not one signed-in account
inboxes.p: A built-in connector follows the account you signed in with, so the assistant sees one identity. Here an inbox is a resource inside a workspace. One agent can read your support address, reply from your own, and file a message in a shared mailbox in a single conversation, and a team can share the same inboxes.

portable.p: A connector a vendor builds runs inside that vendor's app, by definition. This is a standard streamable-http MCP server with OAuth 2.1, DCR and PKCE, so the same inboxes work in Claude, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT, n8n and any other MCP client. Changing assistant costs you nothing.

control.p: Credentials are encrypted at rest in your own workspace, scoped per API key, revocable in one click, and every call is written to an audit trail. The source is public, so you can read exactly what runs, or host the whole server yourself.

faq.title: Native connectors vs MCP, answered
faq.sub: The questions people ask when they are choosing between the two.

items.q: Can my assistant already reach my mail without this?
items.a: If your assistant ships a connector for your mail provider and it does what you need, use it. That is the shortest path. This exists for the mailboxes a built-in connector does not reach, for working across several inboxes at once, and for keeping one setup that follows you from one AI client to the next.

Gmail over OAuth, and any mailbox that speaks IMAP and SMTP. That includes Fastmail, iCloud, Yahoo, Zoho, Yandex, Migadu, a mailbox your company runs, and one you host yourself. You connect it with an app password or ordinary IMAP credentials.

items.q: Can it send, or does it only draft?
items.a: It sends, replies, forwards, schedules for later, moves, copies, flags, archives and deletes. You decide which of those any given API key is allowed to do, so you can start read-only and widen the scopes once you trust the setup.

items.q: Can I connect more than one inbox?
items.a: Yes, as many as you like. Inboxes belong to a workspace rather than to a single sign-in, so one agent can work across several of them in the same conversation, and the people in a workspace can share them.

items.q: If I set this up for Claude, does it work in Cursor or ChatGPT too?
items.a: Yes. This is a standard streamable-http MCP server with OAuth 2.1, DCR and PKCE, so one setup works across Claude, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT, Windsurf, n8n, Make and any MCP client. A connector built into an assistant runs inside that assistant.

items.q: Is it private if a third party connects my inbox?
items.a: The mail your agent reads is fetched live from your provider and never stored on our servers. Only an encrypted OAuth token or app password is kept so future requests can authenticate, and you can revoke access in one click.
